edges.description: Most established larval cysts grow in the liver.
Some established larval cysts grow in the lungs.
Larval Echinococcus cysts most commonly develop in the liver.
A hepatic cyst can rupture or leak, releasing its contents into surrounding structures and the systemic circulation.
Pulmonary larval cyst growth produces lung cysts.
The IgE response to released hydatid antigen most frequently presents as hives.
The same IgE-mediated allergic reaction also presents with flushing.
A major cyst rupture provokes a life-threatening IgE-mediated anaphylactic reaction.
Rupture releases viable protoscolices and cystic contents that can implant elsewhere and establish new cyst foci.

evidence.snippet: A major rupture can cause a life-threatening anaphylactic reaction.

nodes.description: After humans ingest dog-associated E. granulosus eggs, larval metacestodes establish hydatid cysts in susceptible organs.

evidence.snippet: Dogs and other canids harboring gut-resident tapeworms readily transmit the tapeworm eggs (and subsequent formation of larval cysts) to humans in close contact with them.

Cyst rupture or leakage can cause immunologic symptoms from the initiation of an immunoglobulin (Ig)E response, leading to allergic reactions most frequently characterized by hives, flushing, and mucous membrane swelling.

nodes.description: Rupture or leakage of a cyst releases hydatid antigens that trigger an IgE-mediated immune response and can also seed viable cystic material beyond the original site.

evidence.snippet: Cyst rupture or leakage can cause immunologic symptoms from the initiation of an immunoglobulin (Ig)E response, leading to allergic reactions most frequently characterized by hives, flushing, and mucous membrane swelling.

nodes.description: Viable cystic contents and protoscolices released by a ruptured cyst can implant in the peritoneum (or biliary tree), establishing new hydatid foci distinct from the original cyst.

evidence.snippet: Ruptured cysts can release viable cystic contents and protoscolices into the peritoneum, resulting in secondary hyatidosis.

nodes.description: Hives are the most frequently reported manifestation of the IgE-mediated allergic response to hydatid antigen released by cyst rupture or leakage.
